summary:
Pskov Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where the legal and physical risks facing transgender visitors have sharpened markedly since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; the Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" statute criminalises public expression that includes, expressly, anything "justifying" gender transition.

Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation. Official national government warnings state this directly to LGBT travellers, and the US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers. A trans visitor to Pskov Oblast therefore enters under national rules that reach personal expression, documents and conduct simultaneously.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025; assessment updated 11 June 2025) is the baseline against which this region is scored, and it records no deviation: same-sex activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and no specific legal protections exist. The note contains no findings specific to Pskov Oblast or to the Northwestern Federal District, so no regional relief from the national position is documented.

Penalties under that baseline are severe. The 'gay propaganda' statute carries administrative fines, with repeat offences punishable by up to 4 years in prison. The 2023 extremist designation carries 2 to 6 years for participating in the designated organisation and 6 to 10 years for organising it. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism convictions tied to the International LGBT Movement.

Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under that designation; one died by suicide in pretrial detention and courts sentenced two to prison. In the same period 81 people across 98 cases were found guilty under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned symbols, a provision Human Rights Watch links to penalties of up to 12 years in prison. The UK Home Office note counts at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions.

The same Home Office note, in version 2.0 (page updated 12 August 2026), affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement volume is rising alongside severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget across the two preceding years.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, including a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the designation.

Deaths in custody and physical coercion form part of the record. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Participation in the designated extremist organisation carries 2 to 6 years' imprisonment and organising it 6 to 10 years, while repeated 'gay propaganda' offences carry up to 4 years. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions.

Article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses penalises displaying banned symbols; 81 people were found guilty in 98 such cases between January 2024 and June 2025, and Human Rights Watch records exposure to up to 12 years in prison in connection with extremist participation. At least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation in that window, with two prison sentences imposed and one defendant dying by suicide in pretrial detention. By 30 June 2025 courts had issued 101 extremism convictions tied to the International LGBT Movement.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been unavailable since the 2023 legislation barring gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents. Russian LGBT+ people, including those in the autonomous republic of Chechnya, are recognised as a particular social group under the refugee convention in the UK Home Office country policy and information note (version 2.0, page updated 12 August 2026), which governs UK asylum assessments.
outOfScopeNotes:
No enforcement records specific to Pskov Oblast or to the Northwestern Federal District were sourced; the UK Home Office note contains no such findings, and regional deviation from the national baseline is therefore unresolved rather than documented as absent in practice.

The statutory provision underlying the "up to 12 years" figure attached to article 20.3-related extremist liability is not identified in the inventory, so which offence grade produces that maximum remains unresolved.

Entry, visa and border-screening treatment of mismatched identity documents for transgender travellers entering Russia at Pskov checkpoints is not sourced here, as is the availability of competent healthcare for trans visitors within the oblast.

Two versions of the UK Home Office note are referenced across this record (June 2025 with assessment updated 11 June 2025, and version 2.0 with page updated 12 August 2026); whether their substantive findings differ is unresolved.
